name: Active Scanning
description: An adversary probes victim infrastructure directly, sending traffic to enumerate open ports, live hosts and running service versions before committing to an intrusion. Unlike passive collection this leaves records in perimeter logs. Scans are often distributed across source addresses or spread over days to stay under per-source rate thresholds.
detection: Look for a single source touching many destination ports or many destination addresses in a short window, and for connection attempts that are overwhelmingly refused or reset. Flow-level fan-out counters are usually a better signal than any individual connection.

name: Gather Victim Host Information
description: Collection of details about victim hosts such as operating system, hardware, installed software and client configuration, gathered either passively from published artifacts or actively from service banners and error pages.
detection: Largely invisible when passive. Active variants show as unusual HTTP header probing, malformed requests intended to provoke verbose errors, or repeated requests for version-disclosing endpoints.

name: Gather Victim Identity Information
description: Collection of employee names, email address formats, job titles and credentials exposed in prior third-party breaches. This is what makes a later phishing or password-spraying campaign accurate rather than generic.
detection: Not observable on the victim network. Detection depends on monitoring credential-dump marketplaces for the organisation's own domain and correlating exposed accounts with subsequent authentication attempts.

name: Gather Victim Network Information
description: Mapping of the victim's address ranges, domain names, DNS records, trust relationships and network topology, typically from registries and public DNS rather than from the victim's own systems.
detection: Bulk or recursive DNS queries against the organisation's zones from a single resolver, and certificate-transparency lookups for newly issued subdomains, are the usual observable traces.

name: Acquire Infrastructure
description: Purchase or rental of domains, virtual servers, serverless functions or web services that will be used for staging, command and control, or exfiltration. Adversaries prefer infrastructure whose reputation is clean and whose registration details are obscured.
detection: Outbound connections to very recently registered domains, to hosting providers the organisation has no business relationship with, or to look-alike domains of the organisation's own brand.

name: Obtain Capabilities
description: Acquisition of malware, exploits, code-signing certificates or offensive tooling rather than developing it. The practical effect for defenders is that commodity tooling appears in the hands of otherwise unsophisticated actors.
detection: Hash and certificate reputation on newly executed binaries, and detection content for well-known offensive frameworks, cover most of this in practice.

name: Phishing
description: Delivery of a malicious attachment, link or instruction by electronic message to obtain credentials or execution on a user endpoint. Phishing remains the single most common documented entry vector for mid-market intrusions because it targets the one component that cannot be patched.
detection: Correlate mail-gateway verdicts with endpoint process ancestry: a document reader or mail client spawning a script interpreter shortly after message delivery is the highest-value signal available. First-time sender combined with display-name impersonation of an internal executive is a strong secondary indicator.

name: Spearphishing Attachment
description: A targeted message carrying a file whose opening leads to execution, historically through macros, and now more often through container formats such as ISO, IMG, LNK or OneNote attachments that sidestep mark-of-the-web propagation.
detection: Office or archive applications writing then launching executable content, and mounted disk-image files appearing in a user's download path, are the two most reliable traces.

name: Spearphishing Link
description: A targeted message containing a URL that leads to a credential-harvesting page or a drive-by download. Modern kits proxy the real login page in real time so that the session cookie captured after a successful multi-factor prompt is immediately usable.
detection: Web-proxy requests to newly registered or newly categorised domains within minutes of message delivery, followed by an authentication from an unfamiliar autonomous system with an impossible travel profile.

name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
description: Exploitation of a weakness in an internet-reachable application or appliance to gain execution inside the perimeter. Edge devices such as VPN concentrators, file-transfer appliances and management interfaces are disproportionately represented because they are reachable by definition and are often outside the endpoint-agent footprint.
detection: Web-server or appliance processes spawning shells, writing to web-root directories, or making outbound connections they have never made before. Exploitation attempts are noisy in request logs; successful exploitation is quiet, so post-exploitation behaviour is the signal that matters.

name: External Remote Services
description: Use of externally exposed remote-access services such as VPN, RDP gateways, Citrix or SSH with valid credentials to enter or re-enter an environment. It requires no exploit and produces authentication events that look legitimate in isolation.
detection: Successful remote-access authentication from an unfamiliar geography or hosting provider, accounts authenticating outside their historical hours, and concurrent sessions for one account from two networks.

name: Valid Accounts
description: Use of legitimate credentials for access, persistence and escalation at once. Because the resulting activity is authorised, signature-based controls have nothing to fire on, and the only available discriminator is behavioural deviation from the account's own history.
detection: Baseline each account on source network, hours, accessed hosts and volume, then alert on deviation rather than on the authentication itself. Service accounts are especially tractable because their legitimate behaviour is narrow and machine-regular.

name: Cloud Accounts
description: Abuse of cloud or federated identities, including access keys committed to source control and OAuth tokens granted to a malicious application. A single over-permissioned cloud identity often reaches more data than a compromised endpoint ever could.
detection: Control-plane API calls from new regions or user agents, long-dormant access keys suddenly active, and consent grants to third-party applications that no administrator requested.

name: Supply Chain Compromise
description: Manipulation of a product or its delivery mechanism before it reaches the victim, so that the trusted update or trusted dependency is itself the intrusion. Third-party involvement in confirmed breaches has risen sharply across recent industry reporting, and these incidents have the longest measured containment times of any category because the malicious artifact is signed, expected and deployed deliberately.
detection: Cannot be detected at the point of installation, because installation is authorised. Detection requires deviation monitoring after deployment: a build agent or updater process making network connections or spawning children it has no history of.

name: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
description: Insertion of malicious code into a library, package or build tool that downstream projects consume. Variants include typosquatting a popular name, hijacking an abandoned maintainer account, and dependency confusion where an internal package name is claimed on a public registry so the resolver prefers the attacker's higher version.
detection: Install-time scripts making network connections, lockfile changes that introduce an unexpected registry or version, and packages whose maintainer set changed immediately before a release. Transitive depth matters: the risky package is rarely the one named in the manifest.

name: Compromise Software Supply Chain
description: Modification of a software product at the vendor before distribution, typically by compromising the build or signing pipeline so the backdoored artifact carries a valid signature. The malicious code then arrives through the vendor's own update channel.
detection: Behavioural baselines on the vendor's own binaries. A management agent or updater that begins resolving unfamiliar domains, or that loads a module it has never loaded, is the observable part; the signature check will pass.

name: Trusted Relationship
description: Abuse of the access a third party legitimately holds into the victim environment, such as a managed service provider's remote-management tooling or a contractor's VPN account. The victim inherits the security posture of every party holding standing access.
detection: Treat partner accounts as a separate population with their own baselines. Remote-management tooling executing outside a scheduled maintenance window, or reaching hosts outside the contracted scope, are the practical triggers.

name: Drive-by Compromise
description: Compromise through ordinary web browsing, where a visited site delivers an exploit or a coerced download. Watering-hole variants compromise a site the target population is known to visit rather than the target directly.
detection: Browser processes spawning script interpreters or writing executables, and browser child processes with unusual command lines, are the reliable host-side indicators.

name: Replication Through Removable Media
description: Spread by copying malicious code to removable drives, often with a shortcut or autorun-style lure, so the payload crosses network boundaries including air gaps.
detection: Executable or shortcut files written to removable volumes shortly after mount, and processes whose image path resolves to a removable drive letter.

name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
description: Execution of adversary commands through a built-in interpreter such as a shell, PowerShell or a scripting runtime. Using the interpreter already present avoids dropping a detectable binary and is the most common execution mechanism across nearly every intrusion set.
detection: Command-line content is the richest available telemetry. Score on parent-child pairs that should not occur, on encoded or obfuscated arguments, and on interpreters invoked by non-interactive parents.

name: PowerShell
description: Use of PowerShell for execution, download and in-memory loading. Its deep platform integration means most administrative actions have a PowerShell equivalent, so adversary use blends with legitimate automation.
detection: Enable script-block logging; it survives obfuscation because the engine logs the deobfuscated block. Alert on encoded command arguments, download cradles, and PowerShell launched by a document reader or mail client.

name: Windows Command Shell
description: Use of the Windows command interpreter for execution, frequently as the first stage that launches something else or as the harness for chained discovery commands.
detection: Chained discovery commands in a single command line, and the command interpreter spawned by a service, a web server or an Office application.

name: Unix Shell
description: Use of a Unix shell for execution, including reverse shells established from a compromised service back to adversary infrastructure.
detection: Shells whose standard streams are attached to a socket, shells parented by a web server or database process, and interactive shells on hosts that have no interactive users.

name: JavaScript
description: Execution through a JavaScript or JScript engine, whether in the browser, through a Windows scripting host, or in a server-side runtime.
detection: Script-host processes launched with file arguments from user download paths, and server runtimes executing code written outside the deployment pipeline.

name: Exploitation for Client Execution
description: Exploitation of a vulnerability in client software such as a browser, document reader or archive utility to gain execution when the user merely opens content.
detection: Client applications crashing and then spawning children, or spawning children at all when they normally do not. Exploit attempts often leave a crash artifact even when they succeed.

name: Scheduled Task/Job
description: Use of the platform's task scheduler to run code at a chosen time or trigger, which serves as execution, persistence and sometimes escalation simultaneously because tasks can run as another principal.
detection: Task or job creation is a low-volume, high-value event on most hosts. Alert on creation by a non-administrative parent, on tasks whose action is an interpreter, and on jobs registered within minutes of a suspicious authentication.

name: Scheduled Task
description: Creation or modification of a Windows scheduled task to execute a payload, optionally under the system account or another user's context. Remote task creation also serves as a lateral-movement primitive.
detection: Task registration events correlated with the creating process; remote creation over remote procedure call is especially notable because it pairs an inbound authentication with a new task on the target.

name: Cron
description: Use of cron to execute code on a schedule for persistence on Unix-like systems, including writes to per-user crontabs and to drop-in directories that are easy to overlook during review.
detection: File-integrity monitoring on crontab paths and drop-in directories, plus cron-parented processes that are interpreters or that make outbound connections.

name: Service Execution
description: Execution by creating or starting a Windows service, which runs the payload with system privileges. This is the mechanism behind widely used remote-administration tooling and behind much hands-on-keyboard lateral movement.
detection: Service creation events naming a binary in a temporary or user-writable path, and service binaries that are interpreters. Correlate with the inbound authentication that preceded the creation.

name: Malicious File
description: Execution that depends on a user opening a delivered file. The technique is not the exploit but the human step that makes it run, which is why it appears in almost every phishing chain.
detection: Process ancestry from an archive or mail client to an interpreter or unsigned binary, with the file's zone identifier indicating an internet origin.

name: Windows Management Instrumentation
description: Use of Windows Management Instrumentation for local and remote execution, discovery and persistence. It is present everywhere, used by legitimate management tooling, and capable of executing on a remote host with only credentials.
detection: The provider host process spawning processes, remote process creation over the management interface, and permanent event subscriptions, which are rare enough in most environments that any new one deserves review.

name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
description: Persistence by registering a program under a run key or dropping it in a startup folder so it executes at logon. It is the oldest and still one of the most common persistence mechanisms because the per-user variant requires no elevation.
detection: Registry writes to autostart locations by processes other than installers, and startup-folder writes of executable or script content.

name: Windows Service
description: Creation or modification of a Windows service so a payload starts automatically with system privileges, providing persistence and escalation in one step.
detection: Service installation events, changes to an existing service's image path, and services whose binary is unsigned or lives outside a program directory.

name: Create Account
description: Creation of a new local, domain or cloud account to retain access independently of the credentials originally stolen, which survives a password reset of the compromised account.
detection: Account creation is low-volume and should be reconciled against a ticket. Alert on creation followed immediately by privileged-group addition, and on accounts created outside the identity-management pipeline.

name: Account Manipulation
description: Modification of an existing account to preserve or widen access: adding it to a privileged group, adding credentials such as an SSH key or certificate, or registering an additional multi-factor device the adversary controls.
detection: Additions to privileged groups, new authentication factors registered for an account that already has one, and new API keys or application credentials on service principals.

name: Web Shell
description: A script placed in a web-accessible directory that accepts commands over HTTP, giving durable access through the same port the application legitimately serves and surviving most credential resets.
detection: New or modified files in web-root directories, and web-server worker processes spawning shells or interpreters, which for a normal application is a behaviour it never exhibits.

name: Event Triggered Execution
description: Persistence by binding a payload to a system or application event, so execution follows normal activity rather than a fixed schedule. Shell profiles, management event subscriptions and application plug-in hooks are common carriers.
detection: Integrity monitoring on profile and hook locations, and enumeration of event subscriptions as a periodic hunt rather than a real-time alert.

name: Hijack Execution Flow
description: Redirection of a legitimate program's execution to adversary code by placing a library where the loader will find it first, or by abusing an unquoted service path. The host process is signed and expected, so the malicious code inherits its reputation.
detection: Signed processes loading unsigned modules from user-writable directories, and module loads whose path is unusual for that binary's history.

name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
description: Exploitation of a local vulnerability to gain higher privileges on a host already accessed, often against a kernel component or a privileged helper service.
detection: Unprivileged processes whose token changes to a privileged one, service crashes that precede privileged child processes, and abnormal integrity-level transitions.

name: Bypass User Account Control
description: Use of an auto-elevating Windows component or a hijackable registry path to obtain elevation without a consent prompt, converting administrator-group membership into a fully elevated token.
detection: Known auto-elevating binaries spawning children, and writes to the registry keys those binaries consult, are the durable indicators.

name: Access Token Manipulation
description: Duplication or impersonation of another process's token to act in that security context, which both escalates privilege and makes subsequent actions attributable to a different account.
detection: Token-duplication telemetry where available, and the mismatch between a process's owner and its parent's owner, which is an unusual state outside legitimate service code.

name: Process Injection
description: Execution of adversary code inside another live process, so the activity carries that process's identity, signature and network reputation. Variants range from writing a library path into a remote process to replacing the mapped image of a suspended one.
detection: Cross-process memory writes followed by remote thread creation, executable private memory regions with no backing file, and legitimate processes making network connections they have no business making.

name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
description: Modification of domain or tenant-wide policy to grant privileges, disable protections or add a federated identity provider the adversary controls, which converts one domain foothold into durable organisation-wide access.
detection: Policy-object change events, new or modified federation trusts, and any addition of a signing certificate to an identity provider. These are rare, high-consequence events that justify immediate review.

name: Clear Windows Event Logs
description: Deletion of Windows event logs to remove the record of intrusion activity. It destroys evidence but produces its own unmistakable event, which is why forwarding logs off-host matters more than protecting them on it.
detection: The log-cleared event itself, and gaps in forwarded log continuity. A cleared log on a server with no maintenance ticket should be treated as confirmed intrusion until disproven.

name: File Deletion
description: Removal of tools, staged archives and payloads after use to frustrate analysis. Because the deletion follows the activity, the surviving telemetry is usually process and network records rather than files.
detection: Deletion of a file shortly after it executed, and bulk deletion from staging directories, especially when paired with prior archive creation.

name: Obfuscated Files or Information
description: Encoding, encrypting, packing or otherwise disguising code and data to defeat static inspection. The obfuscation itself is frequently more anomalous than the payload it hides.
detection: High-entropy command-line arguments, unusually long encoded strings, and section characteristics typical of packers. Deobfuscation-time logging is more reliable than pattern matching the encoded form.

name: Software Packing
description: Compression or encryption of an executable so its real code is only visible after unpacking at runtime, breaking signature matching on the file as distributed.
detection: Entropy and section-name heuristics on the file, and memory-region characteristics after load. Packing alone is not malicious, so it should raise a score rather than fire an alert.

name: Disable or Modify Tools
description: Disabling, unloading or blinding security controls before the damaging stage, including exclusion-path additions, service stops and signed vulnerable drivers loaded specifically to terminate protected processes.
detection: Any change to the security agent's own configuration, exclusions or service state, reported out-of-band. Agent telemetry going silent on a host that is still reachable on the network is itself the alert.

name: Masquerading
description: Making a malicious artifact appear legitimate by copying a trusted name, location, icon or signature attribute, so that a human reviewer or a path-based rule accepts it.
detection: Mismatch between a binary's name and its signature or internal version metadata, and trusted system file names executing from paths other than the system directory.

name: Match Legitimate Name or Location
description: Naming a payload after a known system binary or placing it in a directory adjacent to one, so casual inspection and path allowlists treat it as expected.
detection: Compare image name against expected path for that name; a system binary name running from a user profile or temporary directory is a high-fidelity indicator.

name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
description: Decoding of an obfuscated payload on the victim host, often using a built-in utility so that no decoder needs to be delivered.
detection: Built-in encoding utilities invoked with decode arguments, and interpreters decoding long inline strings, both of which are rare in legitimate administration.

name: System Binary Proxy Execution
description: Execution of adversary code through a signed, trusted operating-system binary, so that application controls keyed on signature or publisher do not block it.
detection: Focus on argument shape rather than the binary: these utilities have narrow legitimate uses, and invocation with a remote URL or an unusual module argument is close to definitive.

name: Rundll32
description: Use of the library host utility to execute a library export, including from unusual file extensions or from a remote location, laundering execution through a signed system binary.
detection: Invocation with a non-standard extension, an inline script argument, a network path, or no arguments at all.

name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
description: Checks for virtualisation artifacts, analysis tooling or unrealistic system characteristics, with the payload staying inert when it believes it is being analysed. This is a direct cause of clean automated verdicts on genuinely malicious samples.
detection: Sequences of environment queries about processor count, memory size, uptime and installed tooling shortly after execution, followed by immediate exit.

name: Subvert Trust Controls
description: Undermining of the mechanisms that decide whether code is trusted, by signing with a stolen or fraudulently obtained certificate, installing a root certificate, or stripping origin markers from downloaded files.
detection: Certificate-store additions, newly seen signing certificates across the estate, and removal of internet-zone markers from files.

name: Reflective Code Loading
description: Loading executable code directly into memory without writing it to disk and without using the platform loader, leaving no file for scanning and minimal loader telemetry.
detection: Runtime-provided load events where available, executable memory with no file backing, and interpreters resolving memory-management functions, which ordinary scripts have no reason to do.

name: OS Credential Dumping
description: Extraction of credential material from operating-system stores and memory so it can be reused elsewhere. It is the hinge of most intrusions: it converts a single compromised host into movement across the estate.
detection: Handle opens against the credential-store process with read-memory access, shadow-copy creation on domain controllers, and access to credential database files outside backup windows.

name: LSASS Memory
description: Reading the memory of the Windows authentication subsystem process to recover plaintext credentials, hashes and Kerberos tickets for accounts that have logged on to the host.
detection: Any process other than a known short list opening a handle to that process with memory-read rights; also minidump writes whose target is that process. This is one of the highest-precision detections available on Windows.

name: Security Account Manager
description: Extraction of local account hashes from the Security Account Manager database, typically by saving registry hives or reading them from a volume shadow copy.
detection: Registry hive export commands, and reads of the hive files through a shadow-copy path, neither of which occurs during normal operation.

name: NTDS
description: Extraction of the entire domain credential database from a domain controller, or its equivalent via directory replication requests, which yields every account hash in the domain including the key that enables forged tickets.
detection: Shadow-copy creation and directory-database file access on domain controllers, and replication requests from principals that are not domain controllers. The latter is close to a definitive indicator of domain compromise.

name: Brute Force
description: Repeated authentication attempts to discover valid credentials, whether by guessing many passwords against one account, one common password against many accounts, or replaying credential pairs leaked elsewhere.
detection: Count failures per source and per account over a sliding window, and count distinct accounts attempted per source. The spraying variant is invisible to per-account lockout thresholds, so distinct-account fan-out is the signal that catches it.

name: Password Spraying
description: Trying a small number of likely passwords across a large number of accounts, staying below per-account lockout thresholds while still succeeding somewhere in a large directory.
detection: Distinct-account fan-out per source address and per time window, plus a low per-account failure count. A source with one failure against two hundred accounts is unambiguous.

name: Credential Stuffing
description: Replay of username and password pairs harvested from unrelated breaches against the victim's services, exploiting password reuse rather than any weakness in the target.
detection: High-volume authentication from proxy or hosting networks with a success rate far below normal, and successes on accounts whose credentials are known to appear in public dumps.

name: Kerberoasting
description: Requesting service tickets for accounts with service principal names and cracking them offline, because the ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the service account's password. Any authenticated domain user can make the request.
detection: Service-ticket requests with weak encryption types, and a single principal requesting tickets for many distinct services in a short interval.

name: Credentials In Files
description: Recovery of credentials stored in configuration files, scripts, source control, environment files or infrastructure templates. This is often the fastest escalation path in cloud environments because the recovered key belongs to an over-permissioned identity.
detection: File-access patterns that sweep for configuration and key file names, and secret-scanning of repositories and build artifacts as a preventive control.

name: Credentials from Password Stores
description: Extraction of saved credentials from browsers, keychains and password managers on a compromised endpoint, which typically yields credentials for services beyond the victim organisation.
detection: Reads of browser credential databases and keychain files by processes other than the owning application, and copies of those files into staging directories.

name: Keylogging
description: Capture of keystrokes to obtain credentials and content that never appear in any credential store, including passwords typed into applications that do not save them.
detection: Registration of low-level input hooks, raw input device access by non-input applications, and steadily growing files in a hidden directory.

name: Forced Authentication
description: Coercing a host or user into authenticating to adversary-controlled infrastructure so the authentication material can be captured or relayed onward to a service that accepts it.
detection: Outbound authentication attempts to external addresses, and inbound authentications whose source does not match the account's normal host set.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
description: Repeated multi-factor push prompts to a user whose password the adversary already holds, relying on the user eventually approving one out of confusion or annoyance.
detection: Multiple denied or expired factor challenges for one account in a short window followed by an approval, especially when the originating network differs from the user's normal one.

name: Account Discovery
description: Enumeration of accounts and their attributes to select escalation targets, typically through directory queries or built-in account listing utilities immediately after gaining a foothold.
detection: Directory queries with broad filters from non-administrative hosts, and discovery utilities executed in rapid succession by one process, which is the characteristic shape of hands-on-keyboard orientation.

name: Remote System Discovery
description: Identification of other hosts reachable from the foothold, by directory query, name resolution or sweeping, to build a target list for lateral movement.
detection: Internal fan-out to many addresses from a workstation, and bulk name-resolution queries from a host that normally talks to a handful of servers.

name: Network Service Discovery
description: Scanning inside the network to find reachable services and versions, which is how an adversary converts a single foothold into a map of exploitable targets.
detection: Internal source addresses contacting many destination ports or many destination hosts with a high proportion of failed handshakes. East-west flow records are the right telemetry; perimeter logs never see this.

name: System Information Discovery
description: Collection of host details such as operating-system version, architecture, patch level and hardware, used both to select exploits and to decide whether the environment is worth continuing in.
detection: Individually benign; valuable only in sequence. Several distinct discovery utilities run by one parent within a minute is the pattern worth alerting on.

name: File and Directory Discovery
description: Enumeration of the filesystem to locate documents, credentials, backups and shares worth taking, often with extension filters that reveal the adversary's objective.
detection: Recursive enumeration with document-extension filters, and one process opening very many directories across user profiles in a short interval.

name: Process Discovery
description: Listing of running processes, frequently to identify the security agent present before attempting to disable it or to choose an injection host.
detection: Process enumeration followed within seconds by a query about a security product's service or an attempt to change its configuration.

name: Permission Groups Discovery
description: Enumeration of security groups and their members, in particular privileged groups, to identify which accounts are worth stealing.
detection: Queries for high-privilege group membership from ordinary user contexts, which almost never occurs outside administrative tooling.

name: System Network Configuration Discovery
description: Collection of addressing, routing, proxy, name-resolution and neighbour-cache information to understand the network position of the compromised host and where it can reach.
detection: Low value alone; useful as part of a discovery burst and when executed by a process with no administrative role.

name: Network Share Discovery
description: Enumeration of accessible file shares to locate data for collection and writable paths for lateral movement.
detection: One source enumerating shares across many servers, and share enumeration from a host whose user has no file-server role.

name: Remote Services
description: Use of legitimate remote-access services with valid credentials to move between internal hosts. Because each hop is an authorised authentication to a service that is supposed to accept it, lateral movement is defined by the pattern across hops rather than by anything wrong with a single one.
detection: Model the normal source-to-destination authentication graph per account, then alert on new edges: a workstation account authenticating to a server it has never touched, or one account reaching an unusual number of distinct hosts in an hour. Chained hops within minutes are the clearest shape.

name: Remote Desktop Protocol
description: Interactive lateral movement over the remote desktop protocol using stolen credentials, which also leaves a full graphical session and its associated artifacts on the target.
detection: Interactive logons to servers from workstation source addresses, sessions outside business hours, and internal remote-desktop connections between workstations, which are rarely legitimate.

name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
description: Lateral movement by connecting to hidden administrative shares with privileged credentials to write a payload and execute it, typically as a service or scheduled task. This is the classic pairing of a credential-dumping step with a remote-execution step and the mechanism behind most human-operated ransomware deployment.
detection: Writes to administrative shares followed within seconds by service creation or task registration on the same target. Either event alone is ambiguous; the pair within one authentication session is not.

name: SSH
description: Lateral movement over SSH using stolen keys, agent forwarding or harvested passwords, often chained through a bastion so each hop looks like normal administration.
detection: New key-based authentications for accounts with no prior key use, changes to authorised-key files, and chained sessions where a host both receives and originates SSH within a short window.

name: Windows Remote Management
description: Lateral movement through the Windows remote-management service, which offers remote command execution over an HTTP-based transport and blends with legitimate remote administration.
detection: Remote-management service processes spawning children on the target, and remote-management traffic between hosts with no administrative relationship.

name: Pass the Hash
description: Authentication using a password hash rather than the password itself, so a credential recovered from memory is directly usable without cracking.
detection: Logon events whose type and package indicate network authentication with a hash, and authentications from hosts where the account has no interactive presence.

name: Pass the Ticket
description: Reuse or forgery of Kerberos tickets to authenticate without the account's password, including forged tickets signed with a stolen domain key that grant arbitrary privileges and long validity.
detection: Tickets whose lifetime, encryption type or embedded account attributes are inconsistent with policy, and service access with no preceding ticket request. Forged-ticket detection depends on comparing ticket contents against what the domain would actually have issued.

name: Lateral Tool Transfer
description: Copying of tooling between internal hosts, usually over file shares or remote-management channels, so the payload is in place before execution.
detection: Executable content written to administrative or temporary paths on multiple hosts from one source in a short window, which is a strong precursor signal for mass deployment.

name: Exploitation of Remote Services
description: Exploitation of a vulnerability in an internal service to move laterally without credentials, which is how worm-like propagation happens inside a flat network.
detection: Service crashes or restarts followed by child processes or new listeners, and the same exploit signature appearing against many internal hosts from one source.

name: Taint Shared Content
description: Modification of files on a shared location so that other users execute the payload themselves, spreading access without any further adversary authentication.
detection: Modification of many files on a share by one account in a short interval, and the appearance of executable or shortcut content in document shares.

name: Data from Local System
description: Collection of files of interest from the compromised host itself, generally after a discovery pass has identified what is worth taking.
detection: Bulk reads across user document directories by a single process, particularly one with no document-handling role.

name: Data from Network Shared Drive
description: Collection of data from file servers and shared drives, which usually holds far more of value than any single endpoint.
detection: One account reading an abnormal volume or breadth of files from a file server, measured against that account's own history rather than a global threshold.

name: Data Staged
description: Aggregation of collected data into one location before exfiltration, which is the last reliably detectable step before data leaves the environment.
detection: Large archives appearing in temporary or public directories, growing rapidly, with no corresponding backup job. This is the highest-value pre-exfiltration signal because it precedes the outbound transfer.

name: Archive Collected Data
description: Compression and often encryption of collected data before transfer, to reduce volume and to defeat content inspection on the way out.
detection: Archive utilities invoked with password arguments or with recursive document paths, and large archive files created by processes that are not backup software.

name: Email Collection
description: Collection of mail content from local stores or mailbox services, including the creation of forwarding or hidden inbox rules that continue to deliver mail to the adversary after access is lost.
detection: Mailbox export operations, new external forwarding rules, and rules that move messages to obscure folders. Forwarding-rule creation on an executive mailbox should be treated as an incident on its own.

name: Data from Information Repositories
description: Collection from internal knowledge stores such as wikis, document platforms and ticketing systems, which commonly contain credentials, architecture diagrams and process detail that accelerate the rest of the intrusion.
detection: Search and download volume far above an account's baseline, and searches for credential-related terms across repositories.

name: Automated Collection
description: Scripted collection of data at machine speed, which distinguishes itself from human browsing by rate and regularity.
detection: File-access rates and inter-access intervals that are too uniform to be human, and enumeration that proceeds in strict alphabetical or directory order.

name: Application Layer Protocol
description: Use of ordinary application protocols for command and control so the traffic is permitted by policy and blends with normal egress. The protocol is legitimate; the pattern of use is not.
detection: Periodicity is the durable signal: near-constant intervals between connections, small and similar request sizes, and a long-lived low-volume session to a single destination. Compute inter-arrival variance per destination rather than looking at any single connection.

name: Web Protocols
description: Command and control over HTTP or HTTPS, which is permitted almost everywhere and often only minimally inspected. Modern implants randomise timing and mimic browser headers to defeat simple periodicity checks.
detection: Client applications with no browser identity making regular outbound web requests, requests whose user agent does not match any installed browser, and destinations with a single internal client and a long connection lifetime.

name: DNS
description: Command and control or data transfer encoded into name-resolution queries and responses, which works even where direct egress is blocked because resolvers are almost always reachable.
detection: High query volume to one parent domain, long or high-entropy subdomain labels, unusual record types, and a large ratio of unique subdomains to that domain. Query length distribution alone separates most tunnels from normal resolution.

name: Encrypted Channel
description: Encryption of command-and-control traffic, either with standard transport security or with a custom scheme, so that content inspection yields nothing.
detection: Certificate and handshake characteristics such as self-signed or rarely seen certificates, client handshake fingerprints that match no installed software, and encrypted sessions to destinations with no reputation.

name: Proxy
description: Routing of traffic through intermediate systems, including compromised hosts and anonymity networks, to obscure the true destination and to reach networks with no direct egress.
detection: Internal hosts acting as relays, which shows as an unusual pairing of inbound and outbound connections on one host, and traffic to known anonymity-network entry points.

name: Remote Access Software
description: Use of legitimate remote-monitoring and support software for adversary access. It is signed, allowed by policy, and frequently already deployed by the managed service provider, which makes it both effective and hard to distinguish from sanctioned use.
detection: Inventory which remote-access products are sanctioned, then alert on any other one appearing at all. Installation of a second such product on a host that already has one is a strong indicator.

name: Ingress Tool Transfer
description: Transfer of tooling into the environment from outside after initial access, commonly using built-in download utilities so nothing unusual needs to be present first.
detection: Built-in transfer utilities invoked with external URLs by non-administrative parents, and executable content written immediately after an outbound connection to a low-reputation host.

name: Domain Generation Algorithms
description: Algorithmic generation of candidate command-and-control domains so that blocking any individual domain has little effect and the infrastructure can rotate continuously.
detection: Bursts of failed resolutions for high-entropy names from one host. The failures are the signal, since only a small fraction of generated domains is ever registered.

name: Web Service
description: Use of a legitimate third-party service as the command channel, so the destination has excellent reputation and is very unlikely to be blocked.
detection: Non-browser processes using collaboration or code-hosting interfaces, and access to such services by hosts with no business reason for it.

name: Protocol Tunneling
description: Encapsulation of one protocol inside another to bypass egress filtering and network segmentation, frequently paired with proxying to reach otherwise unreachable segments.
detection: Protocol and port mismatch, long-lived sessions with sustained bidirectional volume on protocols that normally carry little, and payload sizes inconsistent with the declared protocol.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
description: Sending stolen data out through the existing command-and-control channel, which requires no new infrastructure and no new egress path.
detection: A change in the direction of volume on an established low-volume channel. A beacon that has been sending kilobytes for days and suddenly uploads hundreds of megabytes is the pattern to catch.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
description: Use of a different protocol from the command channel for bulk transfer, chosen because it is less inspected or offers more throughput.
detection: Outbound volume on protocols with no business use, and any host whose outbound-to-inbound byte ratio inverts sharply against its own baseline.

name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
description: Upload of stolen data to a cloud storage service, which is permitted in most environments, encrypted in transit and backed by trusted reputation.
detection: Upload volume to storage providers by processes that are not the sanctioned sync client, and storage-service use by hosts that have never used it before.

name: Data Transfer Size Limits
description: Splitting of exfiltrated data into small pieces to stay under volume-based alerting thresholds, which defeats any control that looks only at single-transfer size.
detection: Aggregate per-destination volume over hours, not per-connection volume, and count of similarly sized transfers to one destination.

name: Automated Exfiltration
description: Automated, usually scheduled transfer of collected data, which produces a regularity that human-driven transfer does not.
detection: Outbound transfers at fixed intervals with similar sizes, especially outside working hours. Regularity is the discriminator: a human copying data produces irregular sizes and gaps, while a scheduled job produces a timing signature that survives changes to the destination and the protocol.

name: Data Encrypted for Impact
description: Encryption of data to deny access and extort payment. Deployment is typically the final step of a longer intrusion that already included credential theft, lateral movement and backup destruction, which is why detection opportunities exist long before the encryption itself.
detection: Mass file modification with entropy increase, rapid rename activity with a shared extension, and shadow-copy deletion immediately beforehand. At this stage detection is damage control; the earlier staging and backup-destruction steps are the ones worth alerting on.

name: Inhibit System Recovery
description: Destruction of backups, shadow copies and recovery configuration so that encryption or wiping cannot be undone. It reliably precedes the destructive payload by minutes.
detection: Shadow-copy deletion, backup-catalogue deletion and boot-recovery configuration changes. These commands have essentially no legitimate interactive use and should page immediately.

name: Service Stop
description: Stopping of services to cause disruption or, more often, to release file locks on databases and mail stores so that encryption can cover them.
detection: Bulk service stops by one process, particularly of database, backup and mail services, in the seconds before mass file modification.

name: Data Destruction
description: Irrecoverable destruction of data or of the systems holding it, sometimes disguised as ransomware when no key exists to recover with.
detection: Overwrite patterns rather than encryption, raw disk writes by unexpected processes, and mass deletion in cloud storage with versioning disabled first.

name: Network Denial of Service
description: Saturation of network capacity to make services unavailable, often using amplification through third-party services and increasingly used as pressure alongside extortion.
detection: Sharp inbound volume increase with low request diversity, and packet-rate anomalies at the edge. Bandwidth is exhausted upstream of the victim, so upstream telemetry is what matters.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service
description: Exhaustion of an application's own resources rather than the network's, for example by abusing an expensive endpoint or a protocol asymmetry, which needs far less traffic than a volumetric flood.
detection: Latency and error-rate increase without a matching bandwidth increase, and concentration of requests on a small number of expensive endpoints.

name: Account Access Removal
description: Removal or lockout of legitimate accounts to obstruct response, typically executed just before or during the destructive stage so defenders lose their own access.
detection: Bulk password resets or account disables by a single principal, and privileged-group removals with no change ticket.

name: Data Manipulation
description: Modification of data rather than its destruction, in order to cause incorrect decisions or fraudulent outcomes. It is the hardest impact to detect because the systems continue to operate normally.
detection: Integrity checks and reconciliation against an independent record; there is no behavioural signal on the host once the write is authorised.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
description: Authentication using material other than a password: a hash, a Kerberos ticket, an application access token or a stolen web session cookie. It bypasses password policy and, critically, bypasses multi-factor authentication, because the factor was already satisfied when the material was issued.
detection: Sessions whose originating network, device fingerprint or user agent changes mid-life, tokens used from a location the account has never authenticated from, and authentication events with no preceding credential prompt.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
description: Circumvention of the mechanisms that mediate privilege elevation, by abusing a misconfigured delegation policy, a setuid binary, or an auto-elevating component, so elevation is obtained without the intended authorisation step.
detection: Elevation events whose invoking user or command does not match delegation policy, and privileged child processes of helper binaries that normally run a fixed command set.

name: Compromise Host Software Binary
description: Modification of a legitimate binary or library already on the host so that adversary code runs whenever it is used. Persistence is inherited from whatever invokes the binary, which for an authentication library or a system service can mean every session.
detection: File-integrity monitoring on system binaries and libraries, signature verification across the estate, and any unsigned or newly signed replacement of a file the operating system shipped.

name: Resource Hijacking
description: Use of victim compute, storage or bandwidth for the adversary's own purposes, most often cryptocurrency mining. The financial impact is direct but modest; the greater significance is that it marks an exploited host that some other actor may also be using.
detection: Sustained processor saturation by an unexpected process, outbound connections to mining pool infrastructure, and in cloud environments a sudden rise in instance count or instance size in an unused region.

name: Input Capture
description: Capture of user input to obtain credentials and content, whether by hooking keyboard input, intercepting credential prompts, or presenting a spoofed prompt that asks the user to authenticate again. It reaches credentials that are never written to any store.
detection: Registration of low-level input hooks, credential-prompt windows drawn by processes that have no business drawing them, and hidden files that grow steadily while a user is active.

name: Indicator Removal
description: Deletion or alteration of the artifacts an intrusion leaves behind: event logs, command history, files, mailbox items and timestamps. It is the adversary conceding that the activity is detectable, which is why the removal itself is often the most reliable detection available.
detection: Forward logs off-host and compare continuity, because an on-host log cannot protect itself. Gaps in a forwarded stream, cleared-log events, and history files truncated to zero are each stronger evidence than the records they destroyed.

name: User Execution
description: Execution that requires a person to do something: open a file, click a link, copy a command into a terminal, or approve a prompt. It is not a software weakness, which is why it survives every patch cycle and appears in the majority of intrusion chains.
detection: Process ancestry rooted in a mail client, browser or archive utility, combined with an internet-origin marker on the file. Clipboard-to-terminal variants are visible as interpreter invocations whose command line matches a known lure format.

name: Server Software Component
description: Persistence by adding a component to an existing server application, such as a web-server module, a database stored procedure or a mail transport agent, so the adversary code loads as part of a legitimate service that is expected to be running.
detection: Enumerate loaded modules and registered extensions for mail, web and database servers and compare against a known-good baseline. New components on these servers are rare, deliberate changes and should always reconcile to a ticket.

name: Create or Modify System Process
description: Creation or modification of a service or daemon so adversary code starts automatically with elevated privileges. It yields persistence and escalation together, which is why it is preferred over user-level autostart whenever the adversary already has administrative rights.
detection: Service and daemon installation events, modification of an existing unit executable path, and units whose binary is unsigned or lives outside a program directory.

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
description: Configuration of the system so a payload executes at boot or at user logon, through autostart registry locations, startup directories, login items or shell extension points. The per-user variants need no elevation, which makes this the most commonly observed persistence family.
detection: Writes to autostart locations by processes that are not installers, and any autostart entry pointing at a user-writable or temporary path.

name: Unsecured Credentials
description: Recovery of credentials that were stored without protection: in files, in environment variables, in process command lines, in cloud instance metadata, or in registry values. It is usually the cheapest escalation path available and requires no exploitation at all.
detection: Processes reading credential-shaped file paths they have never read, queries to instance metadata endpoints from unexpected processes, and command lines containing credential arguments.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
description: Theft of issued Kerberos tickets from memory, offline cracking of service tickets, or outright forgery using a stolen domain key. Forged tickets are the strongest form of domain persistence available because they need no account to exist and no password to remain valid.
detection: Ticket requests with weak encryption types, tickets whose lifetime or embedded attributes do not match issued policy, and service access with no corresponding ticket-granting request. Forgery detection requires comparing ticket contents against what the domain would actually have issued.

name: Impair Defenses
description: Degradation of the controls that would otherwise observe or stop the intrusion: stopping agents, adding exclusions, disabling logging, altering firewall rules, or removing cloud audit trails. It almost always precedes the damaging stage, which makes it a high-value early signal.
detection: Report control-state changes out-of-band, from the management plane rather than from the host. An agent that goes silent while the host stays reachable, or an audit trail that stops being written, is itself the alert.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
description: Transfer of stolen data to a legitimate third-party web service, so the destination is well-reputed, the transport is encrypted and the traffic is permitted by policy. The destination reputation that normally helps a defender works against them here.
detection: Upload volume to collaboration, storage and code-hosting services by processes that are not the sanctioned client for them, and first-ever use of such a service by a server that has no business reason for it.

name: Dynamic Resolution
description: Resolution of command-and-control locations at runtime rather than embedding them, using generated domains, fast-flux records or third-party lookup services, so that blocking a single address or domain achieves nothing.
detection: High-entropy or short-lived resolutions, bursts of failed lookups, and records whose address set changes far faster than the service behind them plausibly would.

name: System Services
description: Execution by interacting with the platform service manager, either creating a new service or starting an existing one, locally or on a remote host. The payload inherits the service manager privileges, which are usually the highest on the host.
detection: Service creation and start events correlated with the initiating process and, for the remote case, with the inbound authentication that preceded them. Services whose binary sits in a temporary path are close to definitive.
